topics.title: What Egyptian Is
topics.short: Egyptian is an Afroasiatic language, related to the Semitic and Berber languages, written for more than 4,000 years.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptian is related to Arabic because Egypt speaks Arabic today. Ancient Egyptian is its own branch of the family; Arabic came with the 7th-century conquest.

topics.title: The Stages of Egyptian
topics.short: Egyptian changed over time: Old, Middle and Late Egyptian, then Demotic and Coptic.
topics.trouble: Students think "Middle Egyptian" means the language of Middle Egypt (the region). It is the middle stage in time.

topics.title: Why Learn Middle Egyptian
topics.short: Middle Egyptian was the classical language: spoken in the Middle Kingdom and used for formal inscriptions for two thousand years after.
topics.trouble: Students expect every text to be in the language of its own time. Temples of Roman date still used (a late form of) Middle Egyptian.

topics.title: Three Kinds of Signs
topics.short: Signs either write sounds (phonograms), write whole words (logograms), or classify a word without being read (determinatives).
topics.trouble: Students think hieroglyphs are picture writing in which every sign means what it shows. Most signs in a text write sounds.

topics.title: Reading Direction
topics.short: Hieroglyphs run right to left, left to right, or in columns; signs of people and animals face the beginning of the line.
topics.trouble: Students start reading from the side the faces point away from. Read toward the faces: they look at the start.

topics.title: Groups and Quadrats
topics.short: Signs are grouped into neat imaginary squares; within a group, read top before bottom and front before back.
topics.trouble: Students read a stacked group bottom first, or read a tall sign after the small signs beside it. Top before bottom, then the next group.

topics.title: Writing Without Vowels
topics.short: Hieroglyphs write consonants only; the vowels of Egyptian words are mostly lost and partly known from Coptic.
topics.trouble: Students treat the vowels Egyptologists add (nefer for nfr) as Egyptian. They are a modern convention for saying words aloud.

topics.title: The Alphabet I: ꜣ j y ꜥ w
topics.short: The vulture ꜣ, the reed j, the two reeds y, the forearm ꜥ and the quail chick w.
topics.trouble: Students read ꜣ and ꜥ as the vowel a. Both are consonants: ꜣ is a glottal sound, ꜥ a sound deep in the throat.

topics.title: The Alphabet II: b p f m n
topics.short: The foot b, the stool p, the horned viper f, the owl m and the water n.
topics.trouble: Students confuse the owl (m) with other birds, and the water ripple (n) with the pool (š).

topics.title: The Alphabet III: r h ḥ ḫ ẖ
topics.short: The mouth r, the shelter h, the wick ḥ, the placenta ḫ and the belly ẖ: four different h sounds.
topics.trouble: Students write a plain h for all four. The marks matter: h, ḥ, ḫ and ẖ are different consonants and different words.

topics.title: The Alphabet IV: z s š q k g
topics.short: The door bolt z, the folded cloth s, the pool š, the hill slope q, the basket k and the jar stand g.
topics.trouble: Students read the hill slope (q) as k, or the door bolt (z) and folded cloth (s) as two different sounds in Middle Egyptian. By then z and s were one sound, written two ways.

topics.title: The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ
topics.short: The bread loaf t, the tethering rope ṯ, the hand d and the cobra ḏ.
topics.trouble: Students drop the line under ṯ and ḏ. Without it, nṯr "god" becomes a different word.

topics.title: Transliteration and Its Order
topics.short: Egyptologists write Egyptian in a fixed alphabet, ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ, which is also dictionary order.
topics.trouble: Students alphabetize transliterations in English order. Egyptian dictionaries begin with ꜣ and put ḥ, ḫ, ẖ after h.

topics.title: Typing Transliteration (the Manuel de Codage)
topics.short: On a keyboard, Egyptologists type A i y a w b p f m n r h H x X z s S q k g t T d D.
topics.trouble: Students type capital letters at random. In MdC, capitals mean something: H is ḥ, but h is plain h; A is ꜣ, but a is ꜥ.

topics.title: Saying Words Aloud
topics.short: By convention Egyptologists say ꜣ and ꜥ as "a", j as "i", w as "u", and put "e" between other consonants: nfr is "nefer".
topics.trouble: Students take the convention for the ancient pronunciation. It is only a way to talk about words.

topics.title: Biliteral Signs
topics.short: Many signs write two consonants, like pr (house), mn (game board), wr (swallow) and nb (basket).
topics.trouble: Students read a biliteral as one sound. Each one stands for two consonants in order.

topics.title: More Biliterals
topics.short: More common biliterals: zꜣ (pintail duck), kꜣ (raised arms), jr (eye), ms (fox skins), ḥm (club), mꜣ (sickle).
topics.trouble: Students mix up the pintail duck (zꜣ) and other birds, or read the eye only as "eye". It writes the sound jr, as in jrj "make".

topics.title: Triliteral Signs
topics.short: Some signs write three consonants: ꜥnḫ, nfr, ḥtp, nṯr, ḫpr, ḥqꜣ, wsr.
topics.trouble: Students read the ankh only as "life". As a sound sign it writes ꜥnḫ in other words too, like "mirror" (ꜥnḫ).

topics.title: Phonetic Complements
topics.short: One-consonant signs often repeat sounds of a bigger sign beside them, as a reading aid: nfr written with f and r.
topics.trouble: Students read the complements as extra consonants: nfr + f + r as "nfrfr". Complements are not read again.

topics.title: Reading Whole Words
topics.short: To read a word, read each sign in order, drop complements, and stop at the determinative.
topics.trouble: Students read determinatives aloud as if they were sounds. A word's sounds end where its determinative begins.

topics.title: One Word, Many Spellings
topics.short: Scribes could spell a word in several ways, with more or fewer complements and different signs.
topics.trouble: Students think a different spelling must be a different word. Compare the transliteration, not the signs.

topics.title: Logograms and the Stroke
topics.short: A logogram writes a whole word by its picture, usually marked with a stroke: the house with a stroke is pr "house".
topics.trouble: Students read the stroke as the number 1. Under a word sign, it means "this sign means what it shows".

topics.title: Determinatives
topics.short: A determinative at the end of a word is not read; it shows the word's class of meaning and marks the end of the word.
topics.trouble: Students skip determinatives, or try to pronounce them. They are silent, but they help tell words with the same consonants apart.

topics.title: Common Determinatives
topics.short: The seated man and woman, the god, walking legs, the man with hand to mouth, the papyrus roll, the house, the town, the hills and water.
topics.trouble: Students confuse the papyrus roll (abstract ideas) with a sound sign, and the hills (foreign land) with the mountain sign ḏw.

topics.title: Honorific Transposition
topics.short: Words for the king and the gods are written first out of respect but read in their normal place: ḥtp-dj-nsw is written with nsw first.
topics.trouble: Students read the signs in written order: "nsw ḥtp dj". The honored word moves forward in writing only.

topics.title: Writing the Plural
topics.short: The plural is shown with three strokes, by writing a sign three times, or with the ending -w.
topics.trouble: Students read the plural strokes as a number 3 or as a sound. They only say "more than one".

topics.title: Masculine and Feminine
topics.short: Nouns are masculine or feminine; most feminine nouns end in -t (the bread loaf): zꜣ "son", zꜣt "daughter".
topics.trouble: Students think every -t is feminine. Some masculine words end in t as part of the root.

topics.title: The Plural
topics.short: Masculine plurals end in -w and feminine plurals in -wt: nṯr "god", nṯrw "gods"; nṯrt "goddess", nṯrwt "goddesses".
topics.trouble: Students write the feminine plural as -tw. The ending is -wt.

topics.title: The Dual
topics.short: Egyptian has a dual for pairs: masculine -wj and feminine -tj: nṯrwj "the two gods", ꜥwj "the two arms".
topics.trouble: Students use the plural for pairs of things, like hands and eyes. Pairs take the dual.

topics.title: The Direct Genitive
topics.short: Putting two nouns side by side means "A of B": pr nsw "the house of the king".
topics.trouble: Students reverse the order, reading "king's house" as nsw pr. The possessed thing comes first.

topics.title: The Indirect Genitive
topics.short: "Of" can also be written with n, which agrees with the first noun: n (masculine), nt (feminine), nw (plural).
topics.trouble: Students make the genitive agree with the second noun. It agrees with the noun before it.

topics.title: Adjectives
topics.short: Adjectives follow the noun and agree with it: z nfr "a good man", zꜣt nfrt "a good daughter".
topics.trouble: Students put the adjective first, as in English. In Egyptian it comes after the noun.

topics.title: Nisbe Adjectives
topics.short: Adding -j to a noun or preposition makes an adjective (a nisbe): njwt "town", njwtj "of the town"; ḥr "on", ḥrj "upper, who is on".
topics.trouble: Students read a nisbe as a plain noun. The -j ending turns it into "belonging to".

topics.title: nb, "Every"
topics.short: nb after a noun means "every" or "all" and agrees with it: tꜣ nb "every land", ḫt nbt "everything".
topics.trouble: Students confuse nb "every" with nb "lord", written with the same basket. After a noun it is "every".

topics.title: This and That
topics.short: pn and tn follow a noun ("this"): z pn "this man"; nn "these" comes first, joined by n: nn n rmṯ "these people"; pꜣ, tꜣ and nꜣ also come first.
topics.trouble: Students put pn before the noun, or nn after it. pn and tn follow the noun; nn (with n) and pꜣ, tꜣ, nꜣ come before it.

topics.title: Suffix Pronouns
topics.short: Suffix pronouns attach to the end of a word: =j "I, my", =k "you, your" (man), =ṯ (woman), =f "he, his", =s "she, her", =n, =ṯn, =sn.
topics.trouble: Students write =f for "she". =f is "he, his"; =s is "she, her".

topics.title: Using Suffix Pronouns
topics.short: On a noun a suffix means "my, your, his": pr=f "his house"; on a preposition it is the object: n=f "to him".
topics.trouble: Students put the suffix before the noun, as with English "his". It always comes after.

topics.title: Dependent Pronouns
topics.short: Dependent pronouns are objects or follow certain words: wj "me", ṯw "you", sw "him", sj "her", st "it, them", sn "them".
topics.trouble: Students use a suffix pronoun as the object of a verb. Objects are dependent pronouns.

topics.title: Independent Pronouns
topics.short: Independent pronouns stand alone, often first in a sentence: jnk "I", ntk "you", ntf "he", nts "she".
topics.trouble: Students use jnk where English says "me". jnk is used like "I am the one" at the head of a sentence.

topics.title: The Simple Prepositions
topics.short: m "in, from, as", n "to, for", r "to, toward", ḥr "on", ḫr "with, near (a person)", ḥnꜥ "with", jn "by", mj "like".
topics.trouble: Students give m only one meaning. Its sense depends on context: in, from, with or as.

topics.title: Prepositions with Pronouns
topics.short: Prepositions take suffix pronouns: n=f "to him", ḥr=s "on it", ḥnꜥ=j "with me"; m becomes jm before a suffix: jm=f "in it".
topics.trouble: Students write m=f. Before a suffix, m becomes jm.

topics.title: Compound Prepositions
topics.short: Prepositions combine with nouns: m-bꜣḥ "in the presence of", m-ḫt "after", ḥr-ḥꜣt "before", r-gs "beside".
topics.trouble: Students translate each part separately. Learn compound prepositions as wholes.

topics.title: The Adverbial Sentence
topics.short: A subject followed by a prepositional phrase or adverb makes a sentence: z m pr "the man is in the house".
topics.trouble: Students look for a verb "is". Egyptian needs none: subject + where is a whole sentence.

topics.title: jw and mk
topics.short: Statements often begin with jw (marking the sentence as a statement of fact) or mk "look!"; mk takes a dependent pronoun: mk wj m pr "look, I am in the house".
topics.trouble: Students translate jw as a word like "and". It has no simple English equivalent; usually leave it out of the translation.

topics.title: The Nominal Sentence
topics.short: Two nouns side by side can say "A is B", and an independent pronoun can lead: jnk zꜣ=k "I am your son".
topics.trouble: Students confuse "A B" (A is B) with the direct genitive "A of B". Context and pronouns decide.

topics.title: Sentences with pw
topics.short: pw "this" makes a sentence "it is A" or "A is B": zꜣ=j pw "he is my son".
topics.trouble: Students put pw at the start. It comes after the first noun (or noun phrase).

topics.title: The Adjectival Sentence
topics.short: An adjective first, then its subject, makes a sentence: nfr sw "he is good"; nfr pr=f "his house is good".
topics.trouble: Students read nfr sw as "a good him". Adjective first, then the subject, is "he is good".

topics.title: Numerals
topics.short: Numbers are written by repeating signs: the stroke 1, hobble 10, coil 100, lotus 1,000, finger 10,000, tadpole 100,000, and Heh 1,000,000.
topics.trouble: Students read numerals by position, like our digits. Egyptian numerals simply add up, largest first in reading order.

topics.title: Counting Things
topics.short: Numbers follow the noun they count: zꜣ 3 "three sons"; ordinals like "second" use -nw: snnw "second".
topics.trouble: Students put the number before the noun, as in English. In Egyptian it follows.

topics.title: Writing a Date
topics.short: Dates give the regnal year, the month of a season and the day: ḥꜣt-zp 5 ꜣbd 2 ꜣḫt sw 10 "year 5, month 2 of the Flood, day 10".
topics.trouble: Students expect a year counted from one fixed point. Years count from the start of each king's reign.

topics.title: The Five Royal Names
topics.short: A king had five names: the Horus name, the Two Ladies name, the Golden Horus name, the throne name and the birth name.
topics.trouble: Students think "Ramesses" was the king's only name. It is his birth name; his throne name was different.

topics.title: Cartouches and Their Titles
topics.short: The throne name follows nsw-bjt "King of Upper and Lower Egypt"; the birth name follows zꜣ-rꜥ "son of Ra". Both are in cartouches.
topics.trouble: Students read nsw-bjt as part of the name. It is a title placed before the cartouche.

topics.title: Reading Royal Names
topics.short: Read a cartouche sign by sign, remembering honorific transposition: jmn written first in Tutankhamun is read last.
topics.trouble: Students read the god's name first because it is written first.

topics.title: The Offering Formula
topics.short: Stelae and tombs begin ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives", to a god like Osiris or Anubis, for the ka of the dead.
topics.trouble: Students translate ḥtp-dj-nsw word for word in written order. The king (nsw) is written first but read last.

topics.title: Bread, Beer and the Voice Offering
topics.short: The formula continues with the gifts: prt-ḫrw "an invocation offering" of bread and beer, oxen and fowl, linen and alabaster.
topics.trouble: Students read prt-ḫrw as "voice". It means the offering that comes forth at the call of the voice.

topics.title: Titles and Epithets
topics.short: Monuments give titles like sš "scribe", jmj-rꜣ "overseer", ḥm-nṯr "priest" and epithets like mꜣꜥ-ḫrw "true of voice".
topics.trouble: Students take mꜣꜥ-ḫrw as part of the name. It is an epithet for the blessed dead, like "the late".
